title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Petya had left his family after their departure from Moscow, joined his regiment, and soon been taken on as orderly by a general commanding a large guerrilla detachment. From the time he received his commission, and especially since joining the active army and fighting at Vyazma, Petya had been in a state of perpetual, blissful excitement at being grown up, combined with a frantic eagerness not to miss any chance for real heroism. He was thrilled by everything he saw and experienced in the army, but at the same time it always seemed to him that the truly heroic feats were happening just where he wasn't. He was always in a hurry to be somewhere else.

When on the twenty-first of October his general had wanted to send someone to Denisov's detachment, Petya had begged so desperately to go that the general couldn't refuse. But remembering Petya's reckless behavior at Vyazma—where instead of riding along the road to his assigned position, he had galloped to the front line under French fire and twice discharged his pistol—the general explicitly forbade him from taking part in any of Denisov's operations. That was why Petya had blushed and grown flustered when Denisov asked if he could stay. Before they had even ridden to the forest's edge, Petya had been telling himself he must follow his orders strictly and return immediately. But when he saw the French, and saw Tikhon, and learned there would certainly be an attack that night, he decided—with the speed at which young people reverse their views—that the general he had greatly respected until now was a worthless German, that Denisov was a hero, the esaul was a hero, Tikhon was a hero too, and that it would be shameful to leave them at a moment of difficulty.

It was already getting dark when Denisov, Petya, and the esaul rode up to the watchman's hut. In the twilight, saddled horses could be seen, and Cossacks and hussars who had set up rough shelters in the clearing were lighting fires in a hollow where the French couldn't see the smoke. In the passageway of the small hut, a Cossack with rolled-up sleeves was chopping mutton. Inside, three of Denisov's officers were turning a door into a table. Petya took off his wet clothes, gave them to be dried, and immediately pitched in helping set up the dinner table.
In ten minutes the table was ready with a cloth spread on it. On the table were vodka, a flask of rum, white bread, roast mutton, and salt.

Sitting at the table with the officers, tearing apart the savory, fatty mutton with his fingers while grease ran down his hands, Petya was in an ecstatic, childlike state of love for everyone around him, and therefore of confidence that everyone loved him back.

'So what do you think, Vasili Dmitrich?' he said to Denisov. 'It's all right if I stay with you for a day?' And without waiting for an answer, he answered himself: 'You see, I was told to find things out—well, I am finding things out. Only please let me into the very thick of it... the real action... I don't want a reward. I just want...'
Petya clenched his teeth and looked around, tossing his head back and waving his arms.
'Into the very thick of it...' Denisov repeated with a smile.

'Only, please, give me a command—some real responsibility so I can actually command something,' Petya went on. 'What would it cost you? Oh, do you need a knife?' he asked, turning to an officer who wanted to cut some mutton.
And he handed over his clasp knife. The officer admired it.

'Please keep it. I've got several like it,' said Petya, blushing. 'Heavens! I almost forgot!' he suddenly cried. 'I've got raisins—wonderful ones, seedless. We have a new sutler and he has amazing stuff. I bought ten pounds. I like having something sweet. Would you like some?' And Petya ran out to his Cossack in the passage and came back with bags containing about five pounds of raisins. 'Help yourselves, gentlemen!'

'Do you need a coffeepot?' he asked the esaul. 'I bought a wonderful one from our sutler! He has fantastic things. And he's very honest—that's the main thing. I'll make sure to send it to you. Or maybe your flints are worn out or used up—that happens sometimes, you know. I brought some along, right here'—he showed a bag—'a hundred flints. I got them very cheap. Please take as many as you want—or all of them...'
Then, suddenly afraid he'd said too much, Petya stopped and blushed.

He tried to remember if he'd done anything else foolish. Running through the day's events, he thought of the French drummer boy. 'It's fine for us here, but what about him? Where have they put him? Have they fed him? Did anyone hurt his feelings?' But having already caught himself going overboard about the flints, he was afraid to speak.

'I could ask,' he thought, 'but they'll say: "He's just a boy himself, so he feels sorry for the boy." I'll show them tomorrow whether I'm a boy! Would it seem odd if I asked?' Petya wondered. 'Oh well, never mind!' And immediately, blushing and watching the officers anxiously for any sign of mockery, he said:
'May I call in that prisoner boy and give him something to eat? Maybe...'
'Yes, he's a poor little fellow,' said Denisov, who clearly saw nothing shameful in the suggestion. 'Bring him in. His name is Vincent Bosse. Go get him.'
'I'll call him,' said Petya.
'Yes, yes, go ahead. Poor little fellow,' Denisov repeated.
Petya was at the door when Denisov said this. He slipped between the officers, came close to Denisov, and said:
'Let me kiss you, dear old fellow! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!'
And having kissed Denisov, he ran out of the hut.
'Bosse! Vincent!' Petya called, stopping outside the door.
'Who do you want, sir?' asked a voice from the darkness.
Petya said he wanted the French boy who had been captured that day.
'Ah, Vesenny?' said a Cossack.

Vincent, the boy's name, had already been transformed by the Cossacks into Vesenny (springlike) and by the peasants and soldiers into Vesenya. In both these adaptations, the echo of spring matched the impression made by the young lad.
'He's warming himself over at the bonfire. Hey, Vesenya! Vesenya! Vesenny!' laughing voices called to one another in the darkness.
'He's a smart lad,' said a hussar standing near Petya. 'We gave him something to eat a while ago. He was terribly hungry!'
The sound of bare feet splashing through mud was heard in the darkness, and the drummer boy appeared at the door.
'Ah, it's you!' said Petya. 'Are you hungry? Don't be afraid—no one will hurt you. Come in, come in.'
('Thank you, sir.')
('Come in, come in.')
'Thank you, sir,' said the drummer boy in a trembling, almost childish voice, and he began scraping his dirty feet on the threshold.
('Thank you, sir.')
There were many things Petya wanted to say to the drummer boy but didn't dare. He stood beside him in the passage, uncertain. Then, in the darkness, he took the boy's hand and squeezed it.
'Come in, come in!' he repeated in a gentle whisper. 'Oh, what can I do for him?' he thought, and opening the door, let the boy go in first.

When the boy had entered the hut, Petya sat down at a distance from him, feeling it beneath his dignity to pay him attention. But he fingered the money in his pocket and wondered whether it would seem ridiculous to give some to the drummer boy.
